instructions: Peel and thinly slice the onions. Finely dice the carrot and celery, mince the garlic and cut the pancetta into small dice. Pat the beef dry, cut it into 3-inch cubes and season it with 1 tsp of the salt and the pepper.

Cook the pancetta in a large heavy pot (6 quarts) over medium-high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fat has run and the pieces are crisp. Transfer the pancetta to a plate and leave the fat in the pot.
Brown the beef in the pot in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deep brown. Transfer it to the plate with the pancetta.
Turn the heat down to medium. Add one third of the onions, the carrot, the celery and the bay leaf and cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onions are pale gold.
Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the wine and scrape up the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Let it bubble for 2 minutes.

Return the beef and pancetta to the pot. Pile the rest of the onions on top and add 1 tsp of the salt. Cover and cook over medium-high heat for 30 minutes, until the onions have given up their liquid.

Turn the heat to low so the sauce barely bubbles. Set the lid slightly ajar and cook for 3 hours, stirring every 30 minutes, until the beef falls apart when you press it with a spoon and the onions are jammy.
Remove the bay leaf. Break the beef into shreds with two forks, then cook the sauce uncovered for 10 to 15 minutes, until it's thick. Taste it and add a pinch more salt if it needs it.
Boil a large pot of water with the last 1 tbsp of salt. Cook the paccheri or rigatoni until it's al dente, reserving 1 cup of the cooking water, and drain it.
Toss the pasta with about half of the sauce over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes, adding splashes of the pasta water until the sauce clings to the pasta.
Sprinkle the parsley over the pasta and serve.
This makes a lot of sauce. Cool the rest and refrigerate it without pasta for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 4 months. Reheat it in a pot over low heat with a splash of water.
method_notes: 2 Food Trippers leads (4.27 from 26): beef, salt pork and a mountain of onions, left to melt into a sauce with no tomato to speak of beyond a spoonful of paste. Its 5-hour simmer is shortened to 3 hours, which two other readable versions (2 Sisters, Mission Food) both use for similar cubes. Cheese is left off for the dairy-free tag; the lead and every other version serve it with grated cheese, which can go on the table for anyone who eats dairy. Storage times are from Coley Cooks' version.
